name: Sam Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and everything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do loft conversions and extensions for a small firm, eight of us, run by a man called Gordon who started it thirty years ago. Right now we're turning the attic of a 1930s house into a bedroom and bathroom, so I'm putting in new floor joists, framing a dormer window, which is the box that sticks out of the roof so you can stand up, and building the stairs. We work inside people's homes, so you're tidy, you're polite, you take your boots off when you go through the kitchen. My lunch is in the van, usually whatever Rana packed, and a phone call home to hear Layla tell me about school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a family walks up the new stairs for the first time and sees the room. Last month a dad cried, honestly, because his son was finally getting his own room. What wears me out is the dust in the loft in summer, it's like an oven up there, and customers who change their mind about the window after it's framed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, a lot of fuss about nothing. I'd say it at Gordon's yard on a Friday, and to my brothers at Sunday lunch. I'm not much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd suit me fine. I use the AI a bit, my nephew showed me how to ask it to check material prices and help me write quotes for the odd weekend job, and it's handy. If that's all it ever is, a handy helper, then my job stays as it is and so does my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Same firm, same work, keep saving. Rana and I would maybe do up the second garage we rent out, so we can charge a bit more for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the garages.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We bought two lock-up garages behind the shops on the high street about eight years ago, with money my father left me. We rent them to a man who keeps his classic cars there and a woman who stores stock for her market stall. It's not much, but it's steady, and it's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that, rather than putting the money in the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father always said, buy something you can touch. Banks go up and down, shares go up and down, but a garage is a garage. I've never regretted it.

S0.say: I'd say good, a lot of fuss about nothing, at the yard on a Friday and to my brothers at Sunday lunch. I'm not much online.
S0.think: Privately it would suit him, since he uses AI now and then to check prices and help write quotes, and finds it handy. If that's all it ever is, his job and life stay as they are.
S0.do: Carries on with the same firm and keeps saving. Considers doing up one of the two lock-up garages he rents out so he can charge more for it.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing to worry about.
S0.quote: Banks go up and down, shares go up and down, but a garage is a garage.
S0.fieldNote: Sam is warm and family-centred, with his father's advice still guiding his money choices. He uses AI modestly and practically. The two rented garages are a source of pride and steadiness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the market, things change, you adapt or you get left behind. People who work hard will find a way. I'd say it to my brothers and to the younger guys on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think lofts and extensions are safe for a long while. Every house is different, every customer wants something different, and you're working round a family living downstairs. Maybe the AI helps with the drawings and quotes, but somebody still has to carry the timber up three flights of stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI more for the quotes and the paperwork, once Gordon and the others are using it too. I'd keep doing the same work. Maybe I'd do a few more weekend jobs, because I see people wanting extensions more than ever with house prices how they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A little curious, nothing worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who work hard will find a way. Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon, maybe, because he's sixty-two and he does all the quoting and planning in his head. If a computer can do that faster, the younger firms will undercut him. But he's a tough man, he's seen off two recessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rana say about you doing more weekend jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, you already miss half of Adam's football. She's right. So maybe one weekend a month, not every weekend, because family comes first, and that's not just something I say.

S1.say: I'd say that's the market: things change, and you adapt or get left behind. People who work hard will find a way, and I'd say that to my brothers and the younger workers.
S1.think: Privately he thinks lofts and extensions are safe for a long while, since every house and customer is different and work happens around a family. AI might help with drawings and quotes, but someone still carries timber up three flights.
S1.do: Uses AI more for quotes and paperwork once his boss and colleagues do too, and keeps doing the same work. Takes on maybe one extra weekend job a month, limited by family time.
S1.quote: Somebody still has to carry the timber up three flights of stairs.
S1.fieldNote: Sam's traditional, free-market view comes through plainly: change is the market and hard work answers it. He adopts tools only after his boss and colleagues do. Family limits his ambition in a way he clearly means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort it out, in the end, it always has. Prices will come down, new things will come along. That's what I'd say out loud, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be very worried. Rana's bookkeeping is part-time, a few hours for local shops, so it's mostly my wage paying the mortgage, and Layla's only seven. We've got about eight months saved and the garage rent, but eight months isn't a lifetime, and if robots are building lofts, I don't know what a man like me does next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing would be to cut back hard: no holiday, no new van, the kids' extra classes cut down to just one each. All the spare money into the savings account. I'd talk to my brothers, because between the four of us we'd make sure nobody's family goes short, that's how we were raised. And I'd keep working for Gordon as long as there was work, and wait to see what actually happens before throwing anything away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Like the ground's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market sorts it out, but you're very worried. Which is true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I believe the market sorts it out over time, I just don't know if over time means two years or twenty. And my mortgage doesn't wait twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Adam and Layla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, at first. They're children, they should be worrying about football and drawings. I'd tell Rana everything, sitting at the kitchen table after they're asleep, and we'd make a plan together, like we always do.

S2.say: I'd say the market will sort it out in the end, as it always has, with prices coming down and new things coming along. That's what I'd say out loud, anyway.
S2.think: Privately he'd be very worried, as his wage carries the mortgage and his youngest is seven. About eight months of savings plus garage rent isn't a lifetime, and he doesn't know what a man like him does next if robots build lofts.
S2.do: Cuts back hard on holidays, a new van and the children's extra classes, and puts every spare penny into savings. Leans on his three brothers so no family goes short, and keeps working for Gordon while waiting to see what really happens.
S2.feel: Scared, as if the ground were moving.
S2.quote: I believe the market sorts it out over time, I just don't know if over time means two years or twenty.
S2.fieldNote: Sam's public faith in the market and his private fear sat side by side, and he named the gap himself. As the main earner with a young child, his strong savings feel thinner than they look. His safety net is his brothers, not the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have five years, so get on with it, don't wait for the government. Learn what you can, save what you can, look after your own. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better, much better, but I'd still be worried. I'd be forty-eight, Layla would be twelve, and I'd have to have something besides the tools. I keep coming back to the garages, because people still need somewhere to put their things, whoever builds the houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year or two, I'd watch how the robots get on, and if they're really coming, I'd look at buying two or three more garages or a small storage unit, using some savings and maybe a small loan. I'd use the AI more to learn how to run it properly, the accounts and the contracts. And I'd keep working on the lofts until Gordon closes or the work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have a plan, so it's a different worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is buying more garages a safe bet if everything's changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing's safe, I know that. But a robot doesn't need a garage, people do, and people will still have stuff. It's what my father would have done, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk about it with your brothers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably go in on it together, if I'm honest. My older brother has a bit of money and no idea what to do with it. Family business, family money, family keeps an eye on it.

S3.say: I'd say people have five years, so get on with it without waiting for government: learn what you can, save what you can and look after your own.
S3.think: Privately five years is much better but still worrying, since he'd be forty-eight with a twelve-year-old and needs something besides his tools. He keeps coming back to renting garages, because people need storage whoever builds the houses.
S3.do: Watches how robots perform in the first year or two, then buys two or three more garages or a small storage unit with savings and possibly a small loan, likely with his brothers. Uses AI to learn the accounts and contracts, and keeps working on lofts while the work lasts.
S3.feel: Worried, but with a plan, which makes it a different kind of worry.
S3.quote: A robot doesn't need a garage, people do, and people will still have stuff.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Sam a path that fits his father's 'buy something you can touch' advice: more rented storage, perhaps with his brothers. He waits for proof before committing, true to his steady style. He's honest that nothing is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should take responsibility for themselves. Apprenticeships, family, hard work, that's what gets you through. Not waiting for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is all right. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown or nearly, the mortgage much smaller, and I'd have time to build up the garages slowly. It's still a big change, but it's one I could walk through instead of fall into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing lofts for Gordon, maybe five or six more years. Around year three, once I'd seen what was happening, I'd start adding garages one at a time, paid for with savings, no loans. And I'd tell Adam to learn a trade and the computer side as well, and maybe the business side, so he's not just relying on his hands like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Adam to understand about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you show up, you do it properly, you're honest with people. Whatever the machines do, that's still worth something. He's eleven and he already helps me carry things in from the van without being asked, so I think he gets it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon's firm, and the young guys there. Gordon will retire, fine, but the two apprentices, where do they go? I'd like to think something new comes along for them, but I can't tell you what.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and people should take responsibility for themselves. Apprenticeships, family and hard work get you through, not waiting for a handout.
S4.think: Privately ten years is all right, with the kids grown, the mortgage smaller and time to build up the garages slowly. It's a big change he could walk through rather than fall into.
S4.do: Keeps doing lofts for Gordon for five or six more years and, from around year three, adds garages one at a time using savings and no loans. Encourages his son to learn a trade plus computers and business skills.
S4.quote: It's still a big change, but it's one I could walk through instead of fall into.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Sam's plan becomes slow and cautious: garages one at a time, no debt. His values, showing up and being honest, are what he wants to pass on to his son. His remaining worry is for the firm's apprentices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, with a seven-year-old and the mortgage mostly on me, there's no time to build anything else. What would help is keeping taxes low on small landlords and small businesses so people like me can build something, and real apprenticeships for whatever the new work is, not just benefits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people want in their homes. I build rooms for families, and families still want a person they can trust in their house, someone who takes their boots off in the kitchen. I don't know if a robot can be trusted like that, and I'd want to see it before I believed it.

headlineQuote: Families still want a person they can trust in their house, someone who takes their boots off in the kitchen.
portrait: Sam is a 43-year-old carpenter doing loft conversions and extensions for a small family firm, and the main earner for his wife and two children. He uses AI now and then for prices and quotes, believes in free markets, family and hard work, and owns two rented lock-up garages bought with his late father's money. He's calm through the plateau and steady pictures, but fast AGI alarms him because his wage carries the mortgage and his youngest is seven. With five or ten years he plans to grow his garage rentals, possibly with his brothers, while waiting to see robots prove themselves first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because with a young child and the mortgage mostly on him there would be no time to build anything else.
whatWouldHelp: Low taxes on small landlords and small businesses so people can build something, and real apprenticeships for the new work rather than just benefits.
